# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Heather and Victor both say they'd pay more once it proves itself in shorter quotes or bigger deals, which is plainly one group, and Samuel's answer is a different objection (his CPQ already does this, so he wouldn't pay at all), so leaving it on its own is right and the group name is plain.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three are real answers about what would make it worth paying more.

whys.g1: Both answers are left on their own with no groups to misplace them into, and that is fair: one asks for a demo with our price book loaded, the other for CRM wiring on live deals, so neither sits wrong and there are no duplicate or vague group names.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; both are real answers about what would take the time to buy.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, idea, then the buyer, which is the order I'd pitch Veles in, but 'How should directors answer?' (24) comes after the interviews are marked sent, when it should be settled alongside 'Who should ask account executives your questions?' (23) before anything goes out.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 show the same kicker and the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so it reads as one question asked twice even if they hold different fields.
founder.missing: Nothing asks about the second half of what Veles sells: leadership seeing how every rep prices, discounts and concedes. The problem and idea steps are framed only around the account executive's quote, so the sales director's own pain (no insight into negotiations, slow ramp of new reps) is never put to them as a problem, only as a buyer. Also missing is what the team quotes in today (spreadsheets versus an existing CPQ), which decides whether we're replacing a sheet or competing with a tool.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It moves sensibly from the cost of the problem today to what it's worth, where the budget comes from, who signs, the CRM check, and finally whether I'd trial it.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing about how our deal approval works today — who has to approve discounts or non-standard terms and how long that takes — which is the part of pricing a quote that actually slows us down.

screens.why1: Right after I listed the CFO and the RevOps lead as the people who have to agree, it makes sense to ask which one to test, since the sales director gets only one question on this.
screens.why2: The title and options are plain, but the intro's "Pick the one role; nothing is reworded here" is Keel talking about itself and took me a second read to see it just means the roles stay as I typed them.
screens.why3: I know who signs off on discount policy in my buyers' shops, so I can pick the CFO without guessing.
screens.why4: The two roles I typed plus "Nobody else" (the director buys alone) cover the real answers, and they don't overlap.
screens.why5: The belief reads "the sales director decides, and the CFO has to agree," which is what I typed, and the bar asks about the last time they bought help with pricing enterprise deals, which matches my product.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? The sales director gets one question about the last time they bought: did the CFO / the RevOps lead / nobody else have to sign off?

screens.why1: Once I've said the sales director buys and the CFO has to agree, asking what slows the deal down is the obvious next thing for an enterprise tool sold into a sales team.
screens.why2: Approvals, security review, procurement and switching are everyday words to anyone selling into enterprise sales orgs, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I live these blockers on every deal: the CRM integration check, finance signing off on discount rules and IT's security questionnaire.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with a 25-word cap, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a fair escape for a founder who doesn't want to test friction.
screens.why5: I typed three blockers and no timing, but the belief keeps only the CRM check and adds an 'about 2 weeks' I never said, dropping finance's discount rules and IT's security review.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a sales director buying this, and roughly how long does each step take (e.g. CRM check, finance agreeing discount rules, IT security review)?

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense to see Keel's list of what has to happen first and the one it will test.
screens.why2: The rows are in a sales director's own words, but the belief line 'would get through a check that it works with our CRM within about 2 weeks, or not need it' is clunky and takes a second read.
screens.why3: A CRM check, discount rules signed off by finance and an IT security review are exactly the steps I see on every deal with a sales team.
screens.why4: The three rows are the hurdles I would name, each distinct and short, and the list can be edited if a team has another step.
screens.why5: These are my three purchase hurdles as I meant them, and the CRM check is the one I wanted tested, with nothing of Veles leaking to the director.
screens.instead: Belief: Most sales directors could confirm it works with their CRM within 2 weeks, or wouldn't need to check.

screens.why1: Right after I listed the three things that could slow a purchase, it's obvious I now pick the one to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: CRM check, discount rules with finance, security review by IT are all the words my trade uses, and days/weeks/months is plain.
screens.why3: I know how long a CRM integration check takes for a sales team my size, so two weeks is my own honest estimate, not a guess about someone else's job.
screens.why4: The three options are exactly the three steps I typed on the previous screen, distinct and in my words, and the unit menu covers the realistic range.
screens.why5: The belief reads back my pick and my 2 weeks faithfully, and the 'or not need it' clause fairly covers teams with no CRM check without changing what I meant.

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs, the price, who must agree and what slows a purchase, asking what first committed step I want from the sales director is the natural last commercial question.
screens.why2: "First real step" with the hint "time, data, money or a signature" is plain to a founder who books demos and runs pilots every week.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask prospects for: a demo, then a trial on one team's live deals, so this is squarely my own sales motion.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a single escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" is the right escape for a founder unsure what to test.
screens.why5: My "try it on one sales team's deals" is kept, but Keel's belief adds "now" and "in most cases", and "one sales team's deals" reads oddly when the buyer runs one team of up to ten; I meant a trial on that team's live deals.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the sales director to take? (e.g. book a demo, run a trial on the team's live deals, connect the CRM)

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, it makes sense to check the step in the words strangers will hear before the commitment belief is set.
screens.why2: "Try it on one sales team's deals" is how a sales director talks about a pilot, and it reads clean on first pass.
screens.why3: A sales director knows whether they would pilot a quoting tool on their team's live deals; that is their call to make.
screens.why4: The step is under nine words, says one thing, and the bar's "probably not or no" share leaves room for the honest no.
screens.why5: It keeps my step, a trial on one team's deals, and leaks nothing of Veles's name or features to the director.
screens.instead: Try it on your team's live deals for a month.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, and just before strangers see the study, it is obvious to ask whether to invite yes-sayers to a pilot; a trial on one team's deals is exactly what I'd book from a demo.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is everyday enterprise-sales language to me, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads for a live-deal trial is my own call, and I know I do.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, and the two chips are distinct and plain.
screens.why5: The hint's generic "Would you try this for real?" drops the step I typed, "try it on one sales team's deals", so the offer reads looser than a scoped one-team trial.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you try this on one sales team's deals? Leave your work email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, credits, recording once and text messages into one block, so I'd need a second read to see that 400 credits is the same whichever I pick.
screens.why3: As the founder I can decide which voice my account executives hear from what I know of them; I just listen and pick.
screens.why4: Two named voices with previews are distinct, but only names and a 5-second play give me nothing to choose on (tone, accent, formality for a US enterprise sales audience), and there's no 'either is fine' chip even though one is preselected.
screens.why5: My audience, account executives, is kept as typed, and nothing of Veles or the sales director leaks into the interviewer choice.
screens.instead: Who should ask account executives your questions? (Daphne — warm, US accent ▶ 5 s · Saskia — crisp, US accent ▶ 5 s) — hint: one recording for this project, 400 credits either way; people can talk, type or tap.

screens.why1: Account executives and sales directors get separate links, so after choosing who asks the account executives, it makes sense to choose how the directors answer theirs.
screens.why2: The choice reads clearly, but 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' leaves me unsure whether Daphne's video is still being made or something of mine is, and the '9 in 10 where it is loud' line needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know my buyers are VPs and sales directors who skim on a laptop between calls, so I can pick text from what I know of them.
screens.why4: AI video, read-and-tap, or let them pick covers every real choice, the three don't overlap, and each states when it is ready.
screens.why5: 'Directors' matches the sales directors I named as the buyer, and nothing about Veles leaks into this setup screen.
screens.instead: How should sales directors answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (her video is still being made, ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready when Daphne's video is)

screens.why1: Once the directors' interview mode is set, the obvious last step is deciding how the links reach people, so it belongs here as the final screen.
screens.why2: Each label runs straight into its description ("People I know by name I send each one their own link") and the question never says whether these links are for my account executives, my sales directors or both, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching AEs and directors I've met through demos and design partners or posting in a RevOps or sales community, so I can answer this from what I do.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel contact list, one open link posted where the group already is) are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach reps and directors, and I picked the first one easily.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks and the mechanics are right, but after two screens about two separate groups (AEs, then directors) the bare "Who gets a link?" drops which group this is for.
screens.instead: Who gets a link — the account executives, the sales directors, or both? (People I know by name: I send each their own link / People I found with Keel: pick a list from Contacts / A group: I post one open link where they already are)

screens.why_b1: The verdict line says Did not hold and names its deciding number, Purchase friction at 3 of 8 expecting longer than 2 weeks, right under the title, and the rule line says the stage takes its worst card.
screens.why_b2: The tally adds up to my six cards and each card shows its count against its bar, but the denominators move: 7 on existing sacrifice, 5 on ability to pay, 8 elsewhere, all beside '8 people answered'. Why it's 5 on ability to pay takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the names and lines I checked word for word, and the other cards are in my own terms: deals per sales team, $250 to $500, the sales director.
screens.why_b4: The line under the verdict only says who the money questions went to; nothing tells me what one director too many on the CRM check means for Veles or what to change, such as showing the CRM integration working in the demo.
screens.why_b5: n is visible on every card and the price split isn't oversold, but with only 8 directors three cards are called Holding up while sitting exactly at the bar, and the screen never says the sample is small or that one person moves each verdict.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one director: 3 of 8 expect the CRM check to take 2 weeks to a month against your 2 weeks. Show the CRM integration live in the demo so it isn't a separate check. And with only 8 answering, existing sacrifice, buyer and payer, and commitment each hold at the bar with no margin.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 lose 2 or more deals per sales team a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: Seven counted and my bar at 5 of 7 are plain, but the axis counts deals (0 to 6) while the bar counts people, and the unit label 'deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month' is printed twice, so I had to look again to see what the strip counts.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice and my 2-to-4 deals lost or signed on worse terms because pricing was done by hand are my own figure and my own words.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the cost is real for most sales directors and that the open question is whether they would pay to remove it, on the Price card next.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group and a lean, but the So line then says flatly 'The cost is there', when the result sits exactly at the bar and one answer either way would flip it.
screens.instead: Just at your bar: 5 of 7 sales directors lost 2 or more deals last month to hand-worked pricing, so one answer either way flips it; a lean that the cost is real, not proof. Whether they'd pay to remove it is the Price card, next.

screens.why_b1: The count is right beside the verdict (5 of 8 at $250 or more, bar 6 of 8, 1 short), but the status word 'People disagree' never says plainly whether my price belief held or did not, and the stage page put the miss on Purchase friction, so I am left inferring.
screens.why_b2: Price bins with for and against on each, 8 people, my $250 to $500 marked on its bin and the bar at 6 of 8 drawn on the strip: all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Price, per sales team a month, $250 to $500, sales directors: that is my plan band in my unit, the one I priced at launch.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab, even though the three quotes right here already say what to do: prove it shortens quotes for small teams, and don't sell into teams whose CPQ already quotes.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 and 'a lean, not a call' are honest, but 'would pay your price' turns a 'what is it worth' answer into a purchase, and the 3 'who would not' include Heather, who says she'd move up a plan once it is proven.
screens.instead: Not held, 1 short: 5 of 8 directors put Veles at $250 or more a month per team. Two of the three below are small teams who want proof it shortens quotes first, and one already quotes in a CPQ. Lead small teams with a trial on live deals before asking $250.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right next to the deciding number, '3 of 5 from money already there · bar 4 of 5 · 1 short', so I know it missed my bar by one person and why.
screens.why_b2: It plainly counts where the money would come from, over the 5 directors who named my price or more, and the bar sits at 4 of 5 with the marker on the strip; the only small snag is that the 'for' and 'against' rows alternate rather than group.
screens.why_b3: The $250 to $500 per sales team a month is my number, but I never checked an Ability to pay line on the way in; this is Keel's framing of my price, recognisable but not one I typed.
screens.why_b4: 'Expect some deals to need new sign-off. Ask which budget line on the next calls' tells me to plan for a sign-off step and probe the budget source in my demos, which is concrete enough to act on.
screens.why_b5: n=5 stays visible, it says why 3 were not asked, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps it from overclaiming.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one: 3 of 5 had a budget line already, 2 needed a new one signed off (one of them at $500+), so ask on calls whether the CFO signs a new line, which ties to your buyer belief.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, at the bar, so I know my belief held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the eight directors' answers to who signs off. Each bar is marked for or against, and the strip puts the marker at 6 of 8. I read it on first look.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, with "The sales director decides, and the CFO has to agree," is the belief I checked word for word.
screens.why_b4: Plan for the CFO in most deals is concrete: the CFO goes into my sales motion and my discount-rules pitch. The 1 of 8 who could sign alone is a fact rather than an action, but it is harmless.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and the line says a small group: a lean, not a call. The status is the mild Holding up, not strong, which is honest for a result sitting exactly at the bar.
screens.instead: Plan for the CFO in most deals; for the 2 of 8 where several people or someone else decides, ask who signs before the demo.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 expect longer than 2 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bands and the 8 people read at once, but the bar appears two ways ("no more than 2 of 8" against in the verdict, "6 of 8" for on the strip, plus "1 in 3"), and my 2 weeks falls on the low edge of an against band, so I have to stop and check whether a clean two-week check counts for me.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line match what I checked word for word, though the stray line "You said a check that it works with our CRM." reads like a fragment.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a 2-weeks-to-1-month CRM check and points me to what takes the time, and the two quotes (a demo with our price book loaded, wiring it into the CRM on a few live deals first) say what to offer.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the screen flags "a small group: a lean, not a call", and the miss is stated as one person over the bar, not as a rout.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one: 3 of 8 directors expect the CRM check to take 2 weeks to a month (bar: no more than 2); a check of exactly 2 weeks still counts for you, so budget a month and offer a demo on their own price book.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Six for, one probably not, one no, over 8 directors, with the marker at 6, is plain at first look; the bar written as both "6 of 8" and "no more than 1 in 3 against" still agrees.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and carries my belief word for word: the sales director would try it on one sales team's deals now.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is the concrete next step: get the six directors who said yes onto a one-team trial on live deals.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the count line calls it "a lean, not a call", and "Holding up" rather than anything stronger fits a result sitting exactly at the bar.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 would try it on one team's deals, exactly at your bar, so one more no would tip it: book the six into a trial this month, and ask Samuel and Victor what their CPQ or CRM already does that this doesn't.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word with the deciding count beside it: Price 'People disagree' at 5 of 8 against a bar of 6, 1 short, and Purchase friction 'Did not hold' at 3 of 8 against no more than 2.
screens.why_b3: The belief lines are the ones I typed word for word, the $250 to $500 per sales team and the CRM check within about 2 weeks, under the dimension names I checked.
screens.why_b4: The 'Show proof it pays off first' group hints at a move, but nothing says what this means for Veles: run a live-deal pilot with the buyer's own price book loaded, or give small teams a cheaper way in, or drop teams whose CPQ already quotes.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay small and visible (3 against, 2 asked here, 1 asked on Price, groups of 2 and 1), and nothing is claimed beyond the eight directors.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: the RevOps lead, not the CFO, gates the CRM check on live deals; buyers want a demo with their own price book before reps change how they quote; my price is weighed against what the CRM costs; and a team with CPQ sees no slippage on price at all.
screens.instead: Both friction answers ask for the same thing, a demo or pilot on live deals with our price book wired into the CRM, so offer that within two weeks and lead with proof that quotes get shorter for teams under $250; teams already on CPQ are not the buyer.

screens.why1: It makes sense to show me the idea before asking whether I'd buy it, but as the very first thing on the link it lands as a pitch before I know what the study is about.
screens.why2: CRM, CPQ, deal desk, standard terms and discounting are my team's everyday words, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: It's about how my reps quote enterprise deals and what I can see of that, which is my job.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options.
screens.why5: The meaning holds (one place to price, rules and comps built in, less discounting), but the opening line 'a quote built in one place' doesn't say what the thing is, and it only becomes clear later that it's a pricing calculator.
screens.why6: It says mostly fine and C-R-M and C-P-Q say well to a sales ear, but 'one place' is said twice and the deal-desk-rules-standard-terms-benchmarks sentence is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.instead: Imagine Veles, a pricing calculator inside your CRM and CPQ. When a buyer asks for a quote, your reps price it there, with deal desk rules, standard terms and comparable deals built in, and you see how every deal was priced and negotiated. The people building it believe it would mean accurate pricing and less discounting.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what doing pricing the current way has cost me is a natural first question about the buying decision.
screens.why2: It packs two outcomes into one count, lost or signed on worse terms, and 'worked out by hand' isn't how I'd say it; we price in spreadsheets and the deal desk.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many deals slipped or got discounted last month, but saying it was *because* the pricing was manual is a guess I can't really back up.
screens.why4: A number box fits, but 'deals per sales team' is odd when I run one team, and 'None' sitting beside the escape is a second negative rather than a true escape.
screens.why5: It assumes manual pricing is what loses deals, which leans toward the product's pitch rather than asking neutrally about my pricing.
screens.why6: The question says fine, but 'a number of deals per sales team last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, how many of your team's deals were lost or discounted further because the quote took too long to price and approve? Say a number, or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about deals lost to hand-worked pricing, asking what it would be worth is the natural next step for me as the one who pays for our sales tools.
screens.why2: "Worth to you a month, per sales team" is how I already think about a tool line on my budget, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I sign off on our sales stack, so putting a monthly number on a quoting tool for my team is something I do for real.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover where quote and pricing tools land for a team of up to ten, with "I wouldn't pay for this" and "I can't say" both fitting; "$1,000 or more" lumps a wide range but still holds my answer.
screens.why5: It asks plainly what the quote tool on the card is worth to me per team per month, with no product plan or roles of the founder's slipping through.
screens.why6: The four options say well and the two-step split is easy to hold, but "Or say you can't say" sounds clumsy out loud and makes me stop for a beat.
screens.instead: What would Veles be worth to you a month, for your whole sales team? Under $250; $250 to under $500; $500 or more; or you wouldn't pay for this. Or tell me you can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I named a monthly price, asking where that money would come from is the obvious next thing a vendor needs to know from someone who holds the budget.
screens.why2: Budget line, sign-off and taking it from other spending are how I talk about funding a sales tool with my CFO, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I own the sales tools budget, so I know whether this would come out of an existing line, need a new approval or get carved out of something else.
screens.why4: The options slip into past tense for a what-if question, and 'There was no budget for it' is not a source of money, so it overlaps with needing a new line or taking it from elsewhere.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's price question and asks about my budget without leaking any product detail or odd terms for my role.
screens.why6: It is short and the four options are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard, and the past-tense options jar against 'would' in the spoken stem.
screens.instead: You said about $250 to $500 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have; a new line someone would have to approve; moved from other spending; or there's no money for it. Or: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I said where the money would come from, asking whether I can sign off on it myself or need the CFO is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Signing off on a tool spend and getting the CFO to agree is exactly how I talk about buying tools for my team.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and when finance has to get involved, so I can answer this straight from my own job.
screens.why4: The CFO option overlaps with 'several people would have to agree', since the CFO is usually one of those several, and the yes sitting second after a no reads oddly.
screens.why5: I gave a range of $250 to $500, but the question quotes only the bottom at about $250, and 'per sales team' is their unit when I run one team, so it has drifted a little toward their pricing.
screens.why6: It reads as one question with four options I can hold, but 'or say you can't say' trips when heard aloud and the options are long, near-sentence phrases.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on $250 to $500 a month for this yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, on my own · No, the CFO would have to agree · No, the CFO and others would have to agree · No, it's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, asking what would hold the purchase up, such as getting RevOps to confirm it plays with our CRM, is the natural next step.
screens.why2: 'A check that it works with our CRM take before it went through' is tangled; checks don't 'go through', purchases do, so I'd need to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know whether our ops or IT people would need to vet a new tool against Salesforce and roughly how long that takes, so I can answer it.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and don't overlap, and 'It wouldn't be needed' covers a tool that just plugs in; 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: 'Our CRM' is the founder speaking about their own setup; to me it should be 'your CRM', so the founder's voice leaks through.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, 'a check ... before it went through' sounds like a payment cheque clearing, and the stem runs long before the options start.
screens.instead: If you bought Veles, how long would it take to confirm it works with your CRM? Under 1 week · 1 to under 2 weeks · 2 weeks to 1 month · 1 to 3 months · Over 3 months · It wouldn't be needed; escape: I can't tell

screens.why1: After the price, the money, the sign-off and the CRM check, asking whether I'd actually try it is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: Trying a tool on one team's deals is how I'd pilot anything, so I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides whether a team pilots a tool, so I know my own answer.
screens.why4: The options are lopsided: there's a firm yes but only a 'probably not' with no 'probably yes', so if I'm leaning yes but want to see it first, I have nowhere to go.
screens.why5: It still reads as the founder's pilot ask and leaks nothing beyond the idea card I was shown on purpose.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options I can hold after one hearing, and the first option just echoes the stem.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you try it on one sales team's deals, or not? Yes, I'd try it · Probably yes · Probably not · No
